card.hook: Picture a sandstone point, a ferry sliding across the water, and the Opera House and Harbour Bridge sitting side by side like they booked the spot for your photo. That's the classic postcard view, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Stand at Mrs Macquarie's Chair, at the tip of the peninsula on the Farm Cove side of the Royal Botanic Garden, and step a little back from the chair itself so both landmarks fit. The Opera House is about 742 m to the north-west in a straight line, so face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (it depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the sails with a ferry passing in front. Use 0.5x if you step back and want more foreground and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the sky and sails get plenty of room, then tap the sails and slide it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash them out.
card.best_time: Aim for about twenty minutes before sunrise, when the sails catch the first light. In dim light, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked in to hold steady.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the ledge at Campbell's Cove Jetty, on the walk from Hickson Road Reserve to Circular Quay just before the jetty. You'll be in the foreground with the Opera House behind you, and the light is especially good at sunset. Another good spot is the curved harbourside walkway in front of the Opera Bar, which keeps the sails in the background and can be used even when the bar is closed. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the sails over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out front on the city side of the building while you stand on the front steps of the Opera House with the sails behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The garden gates close around sunset, so plan your exit before you settle in for the evening. Check that the Campbell's Cove ledge and the Opera Bar walkway are still open before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a ferry gliding into the gap between the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge, and see if you can get it in the frame before it sails off.
card.good_to_know: Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the international design competition in 1957, and Queen Elizabeth II opened the building on 20 October 1973. Up close, the sails aren't plain white. They're covered in more than a million tiles, glossy white and matte cream, which gives a faint chevron pattern that can catch the light.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: from Mrs Macquarie's Chair the famous Coathanger looks a bit small at first. Don't worry, that's the trick, because it lets you fit the bridge, the Opera House and the harbour into one picture.
card.stand_here: Stand at Mrs Macquarie's Chair, at the tip of the peninsula inside the Royal Botanic Garden (walk out along the shore from Farm Cove). Face out over the water: the bridge lies to the north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the bridge, the Opera House and the harbour all in one frame. Take a test shot, then try 2x if you'd like the arch bigger. Skip 0.5x here, as it makes the bridge look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and run the arch along one of the horizontal lines, with the Opera House off to one side and a bit of water in front.
card.best_time: Sunset and late afternoon are the sweet spot, especially under dramatic skies. Sunrise works too. At dusk, try night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to Hickson Road Reserve in The Rocks, on the waterfront under the south end of the bridge. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the arch rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At Blues Point Reserve in McMahons Point, ask a passer-by to stand back on the little beach that appears at low tide, so they get the bridge square-on with you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: BridgeClimb doesn't let you take your own gear up the bridge, which one blogger says is for safety reasons. Check the official site for opening times, and for any walkway or pylon lookout, before you go.
card.challenge: Tap the bridge, then catch a ferry sliding across the water in a Live Photo with the arch sitting neatly on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: The Sydney Harbour Bridge opened in 1932 and is nicknamed "the Coathanger". Its arch spans 504 metres and rises 134 metres above the water. It's held together by around six million hand-driven rivets.

card.hook: Most people shoot The Rocks from inside it, then wonder why it just looks like a lane of old houses. Climb Observatory Hill instead and the sandstone rooftops fill the bottom of your screen while the Harbour Bridge arches across the back. The short climb puts some people off, so it's often quieter up there too.
card.stand_here: Stand on Observatory Hill, on the west-facing lawn near the rotunda and the fig trees. The centre of The Rocks lies to the east of this point, so face the rooftops and the Harbour Bridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rooftops and the bridge together. Try 0.5x if you want more of the lawn and the fig trees in the frame. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it to pick out the bridge or a cluster of sandstone roofs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge on an upper line with the rooftops filling the lower third, then tap the bridge or bright sky and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the sandstone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour (4-6pm), when the western light falls on the rooftops.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone steps of Argyle Stairs, which climb from the Argyle Cut toward Cumberland Street, with the sandstone walls behind you. Or stand in front of the heritage terraces on Gloucester Street with their arched windows behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so more of the old stone fits in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by and stand on the grass near the rotunda at the top of Observatory Hill, so the rooftops and lanes spread out below you with the Harbour Bridge beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: Observatory Hill is an open public park, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures. Weekends can bring wedding parties, so check your foreground and move a few steps if someone wanders in.
card.challenge: Find a fig tree branch and use it as a green frame at the edge of your shot, with the bridge peeking through the gap.
card.good_to_know: The Rocks was settled shortly after the colony's formation in 1788, first with simple wattle-and-daub houses and later with local sandstone, which gave the area its name. Many of those sandstone buildings are still standing. In the 1970s residents and unions fought off plans to demolish most of the district, which is why the old streets are still here.

card.hook: Down at street level, a cruise ship can park itself right in front of the Opera House and ruin your day. So go up instead and look down on the ferries, with the bridge and the Opera House both lined up behind them.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Cahill Expressway, the elevated walkway above Circular Quay, near the George Street end toward The Rocks. Face out over the ferry wharves and the water, with the Harbour Bridge on one side and the Opera House on the other.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the Quay, the bridge and the Opera House all in one go. Try 0.5x for more wharves and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Opera House or the bridge on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line, so the ferries and water fill the bottom of the picture and the two landmarks sit higher up.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than midday. You're looking north, often towards the sun, so check the sky and tap the Opera House, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky stays blue.
card.selfie_here: Try the ledge beside Campbell's Cove Jetty, on the walk from Hickson Road Reserve toward Circular Quay. Sit on it, use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and let the Opera House sit behind you. One guide says sunset makes it even better.
card.ask_someone: At the Sydney Opera House steps, stand on the steps and ask your helper to stand a little further back, down from the top steps, so the building's full shape fits in the frame. Go early to beat the crowds.
card.rules_and_safety: The walkway is reached by lifts near the station and is understood to be free, but check the official site for opening hours and closures before you go. If it's shut or too crowded, Circular Quay Wharf 3 gives a street-level view of the ferries with the bridge behind them.
card.challenge: Wait for a ferry to slide into a gap between the bridge and the Opera House, then snap it. Bonus points if the ferry is perfectly in the middle.
card.good_to_know: The Quay was built between 1837 and 1844, by reconstructing the southern end of Sydney Cove with an artificial shoreline. The first ferry wharf arrived in 1879, and ferries have ruled the harbour since the 1890s. The Cahill Expressway you're standing on opened on 24 March 1958.

The old Harbourside shopping centre was demolished in 2023, so the view may look a bit different from year to year.

card.hook: From across the water, Luna Park looks like a toy set parked right under the Harbour Bridge. That's exactly why this view works: you get a giant smile, a famous bridge and a big stretch of harbour in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Hickson Road Reserve, an easy walk from Circular Quay. Face north, because Luna Park is straight across the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the bridge, the water and the park all fit. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to bring the park closer, and skip 0.5x because it shrinks the park even more.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line, then tap the park and drag the slider a touch darker so the lights and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Check sunset time for your visit, because the best light changes through the year. Dusk is worth a try if you want smooth-looking water.
card.selfie_here: Head to the approach in front of the Luna Park entrance at 1 Olympic Drive, Milsons Point. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the smiling face and its two towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Lavender Bay shoreline facing Luna Park while you stand between them and the park, so the whole park and the Harbour Bridge fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography on the rides is generally not allowed for safety reasons, so follow the ride operators' instructions. Entering the park grounds is free, and you only pay for rides.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the bridge and the park both look like they're sitting on a thin strip of water, with a bit of harbour left in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: Luna Park opened on 4 October 1935, on a site once used to build steelwork for the Harbour Bridge. The big smiling face sits between two Art Deco towers and has been rebuilt and reworked over the years. The park closed and reopened several times before settling into its current run in 2004.

card.hook: Imagine framing a shot in the middle of Sydney's business district without a single car to dodge. That's Martin Place, and the sandstone arches of the General Post Office make it easy.
card.stand_here: Stand at the General Post Office on the south side of the western end of the mall, with the long line of sandstone arches in front of you. Then turn east and the main stretch of Martin Place opens up ahead.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the row of arches and the wide street scene. Try zoom 2x for the soldier and sailor on the Cenotaph, or zoom 0.5x if the square is busy and you need to squeeze everything in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the columns upright, then tap the arches and slide the brightness a touch darker so the sandstone keeps its colour against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Outside the Christmas period, any time you can get a clear view works. For the wide view with the towers, walk a little east and shoot along the plaza at dusk. From late November to Christmas Eve, go after about 9 PM when the crowds thin out, and skip ANZAC Day mornings if you want the Cenotaph.
card.selfie_here: Stand at ground level beside the circular Lloyd Rees ("Matrix") fountain in the middle of the square, with the heritage bank buildings behind you. Or stand in front of the GPO's sandstone arches for a layered background. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x so more of the backdrop fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Events and ceremonies can restrict access near the Cenotaph, so check the official site before you go. Martin Place has also been a site for protests and demonstrations, so be aware of possible public gatherings.
card.challenge: Get all those arches in one shot, lined up so neatly your gridlines look like they did the work for you.
card.good_to_know: The General Post Office was started in 1863 and finished in 1891, in a Venetian-Italianate style. The mall took its name a year later, in 1892, after Sir James Martin, a former Premier of New South Wales. The Sydney Cenotaph was dedicated on 8 August 1927 and is made of Moruya granite, with bronze figures of a soldier and a sailor.

card.hook: Stand at the bottom of Sydney Tower and your neck gets a workout. The shaft just keeps going up until it ends in a golden turret and a spire, and it's hard to believe it will all fit on your screen.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the foot of Sydney Tower on Market Street, between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so there's no further walk (about 0 minutes on foot). Face the tower, hold your phone nearly upright and tilt it back gently to look up the shaft.
card.zoom: At the base, zoom 0.5x is your friend, because 1x won't fit the whole tower in. For the full-length shot, walk back along the nearby streets until the spire fits, then use 1x. To pick out the golden turret on its own, try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the shaft up with a vertical line so the tower doesn't lean, and leave a little sky above the tip of the spire.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is usually lovely, when the sky has some colour and the tower stands out from it. Early morning tends to have fewer people at the base. After dark, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Cockle Bay Wharf waterfront in Darling Harbour, where the tower rises above the buildings behind the water. It may work for a selfie, but check the view before you line up. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the tower over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed at Sydney Tower Eye, so your phone is fine inside the attraction. The pavements around the entrances get busy, so keep clear of the doors while you shoot.
card.challenge: Take one shot from the base, looking straight up, and one from far enough back to fit the whole spire. Then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: Sydney Tower is the tallest structure in Sydney at 309 m, and you may also hear it called Centrepoint Tower or the Sydney Tower Eye. Architect Donald Crone designed it, and the public were first let in on 25 September 1981. The city's height limit was set lower before it was built, to leave room for the harbour's flying boats. The observation deck sits about 250 m above the ground and needs a pass, and the SKYWALK is only available on booked tours, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the foot of Sydney Tower on Market Street, between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so there's no further walk (about 0 minutes on foot). Face the tower, hold your phone nearly upright and tilt it back gently to look up the shaft.

card.hook: Picture this: the Opera House on one side, the Harbour Bridge on the other, and a ferry sliding through the middle like it was booked for the shot. That's the view from Mrs Macquarie's Chair, and yes, it's the classic postcard for a reason.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Mrs Macquarie's Chair, the sandstone seat at the tip of the peninsula at the east end of the garden, and face out across the water. The middle of the garden lies about 700 m to the south-west, behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge both fit. Want the sandstone seat and a big sky too? Try 0.5x. Or try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to squeeze the two landmarks closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water's edge on a lower line and the two landmarks along the upper third, then tap the landmarks and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning or sunset, when there are fewer tour groups. If you're going for sunset, check the garden's closing time on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the front camera in front of the Calyx glasshouse, with the garden paths and planting behind you. One travel guide calls its bold design a strong backdrop, so switch to 0.5x and let it sit over your shoulder. For softer, shadier portraits, stand under the sandstone archways beside the Garden Café.
card.rules_and_safety: One reviewer advises carrying water and sun protection on hot days. Check the official site for current closing times before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few shots as a ferry passes and pick the one where it lands neatly between the Opera House and the Bridge.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Botanic Garden covers about 30 hectares on the shore of Farm Cove. It opened in 1816 and is the oldest scientific institution in Australia. The first European farm on the continent was started on this ground in 1788, and the garden is free and open every day of the year.

card.hook: The QVB is about 190 metres long, so fitting it into one phone photo is a bit like parking a bus in a shoebox. Good news: the right corner makes it easy.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of George Street and Park Street, on the corner facing the building's George Street frontage. Face north and the Romanesque facade stretches out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole long frontage in. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls don't lean, then let the footpath lead the eye to the facade.
card.best_time: Go outside the busiest shopping hours if you can, so there are fewer people on the footpath. In the evening, try night mode if the facade is lit.
card.selfie_here: Head inside and stand under the upside-down clock, or just behind the staircase, so the mosaic and clock frame you. Or stand next to the stained glass windows by the central staircase with the glass behind you. Use the front camera, and if you want more of the background, try 0.5x. Those spots come from older travel blogs, so look around if things have moved.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the corner of Park Street and George Street and shoot back toward the building, with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is generally fine for personal use, but keep it discreet: no intrusive shots of shoppers and no photos inside private stores. Check for roadworks on George Street before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then one close-up of a single dome. Can you spot both in your camera roll later and still say 'same building'?
card.good_to_know: The QVB was designed by Scottish-born architect George McRae in a Romanesque Revival style and built between 1893 and 1898. It started life as a marketplace and was restored and returned to its original use in the late twentieth century. It's heritage-listed and measures about 30 metres wide by 190 metres long.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of George Street and Park Street, on the corner facing the building's George Street frontage. Face north and the Romanesque facade stretches out in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a nice surprise: from the lawn at the top of this headland, you get two famous bridges in one photo. Anzac Bridge sits off to the west and the Sydney Harbour Bridge to the north.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lawn at the top of the headland, which guides call Stargazer Lawn. The lifts near Munn's Slipway and The Cutaway save you the climb. Walk to the edge of the lawn and face out over the harbour.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both bridges into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Harbour Bridge on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of them, with a bridge on each side and the harbour in the middle.
card.best_time: Sunset is reported to be busy, so arrive early if you want a clear spot at the edge of the lawn. After dusk, switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Try the rock ledges on the middle section of Wulugul Walk. A visitor guide recommends them at sunset for a clean foreground and a wide harbour frame. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the harbour and the bridge sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Drone use is restricted, so check local rules before flying one. Wedding photoshoots need an approved permit, but ordinary walking shots on the wide paths don't, according to one guide.
card.challenge: Get both bridges in one frame with you in the middle, and bonus points if you keep the horizon dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The park is named after Barangaroo, a Kamaraygal woman who was the second wife of Bennelong. The wider area took her name in October 2007. Long before the docks, the Cadigal people used this shoreline for fishing and hunting, and shell middens nearby point to occupation going back around 6,000 years.

card.hook: Everyone queues for the famous stone bench, but the sneaky-good view is a minute's stroll away, down by the water. Same Opera House, same Harbour Bridge, far fewer elbows.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lower walking path on the Farm Cove shore at Mrs Macquarie's Point, just below the chair (the chair is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot). Face across the water so the Opera House and Harbour Bridge sit with the harbour between them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the Opera House, the Bridge and the harbour all in one shot. Try 2x or higher to pick out the Opera House roof shells on their own (higher zooms depend on your phone). Only use 0.5x if you want lots of foreground, because the landmarks will look smaller.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a line, then keep a strip of water or shoreline at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day is usually nicer for colour and softer light, but it's also busier. Check the sun position for your visit before you plan a sunrise or sunset shot.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the carved sandstone seat itself, with the harbour behind the chair, and use the front camera. Hold your phone a bit lower and try 0.5x if you want more of the scene behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the benches in front of the observation deck, facing back toward the chair, while you pose on the seat.
card.rules_and_safety: Access can be tricky after dark or during events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once with a strip of water at the bottom and once without, then see which one you'd actually frame.
card.good_to_know: Convicts carved the chair by hand in 1810 for Elizabeth Macquarie, wife of Governor Lachlan Macquarie. Folklore says she liked to sit here and watch for ships arriving from Britain. The stone inscription above the seat is about Mrs Macquarie's Road, completed on 13 June 1816 and measuring 3 miles and 377 yards.

card.hook: Here's a fun mix: a grand old stone portico with columns, and right beside it, low glass pavilions that look like they landed from the future. Together they make one of the tidiest photos in The Domain.
card.stand_here: Stand on Art Gallery Road at the pedestrian crossing in front of the Art Gallery of New South Wales. The gallery is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot, so face south-east across the road to the columned sandstone front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the crossing, which should fit the portico and the glass pavilions together. If you're stuck close to the kerb, try 0.5x, and use 2x or more for a tighter shot of the columns or the statues.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to line up the columns with the vertical lines, then tap the sandstone and drag the slider darker if the sky is bright and the stone looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day, when the light is soft, suits pale sandstone best. A quieter moment also helps you get the crossing without people walking through.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Art Gallery Road crossing with the sandstone front and its nine steps behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the portico fits over your shoulder, or try the art garden between the two buildings with the glass Naala Badu pavilions behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Art Gallery Road, across the road from the nine steps of the sandstone building, so the whole facade and portico fit in the frame, while you wait in front of the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are for personal use only, without flash or selfie sticks, unless a sign says otherwise, and some temporary exhibitions have extra photo rules. Stay on the pavement rather than the road when you step back for the wide shot.
card.challenge: Find the two horse statues by Gilbert Bayes out the front and get both in your frame with the columns behind them.
card.good_to_know: The gallery began as the New South Wales Academy of Art in 1872. The permanent building was designed by government architect Walter Liberty Vernon, with the first galleries opening in 1897. The two statues by Gilbert Bayes were placed in front of the main facade in 1926.

card.hook: Sydney's glass towers are lining up behind a sandstone clock tower, and somehow the old building still wins. It's a tidy, symmetrical front, so it's one of the easiest grand buildings to photograph in the city.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement directly across George Street from the Town Hall's full front, and face the building so the whole facade and clock tower fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and clock tower in from across the street. If you're further back, zoom 1x looks more natural, with less stretching at the edges. Try zoom 2x or more for the clock tower or the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the facade up with the middle of the frame, so the symmetry really shows.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the sandstone glows in warm light. It's a busy part of town, so wait a moment for a gap in the crowd before you snap.
card.selfie_here: Head up the Town Hall front steps on George Street and turn so the sandstone facade is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt the phone slightly up so the grand entrance stays over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand on the footpath opposite the building on George Street while you pose on the front steps, so they can frame the full front of the Town Hall.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the facade from the public pavement on George Street, but opening hours and access inside vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the clock tower is dead centre and perfectly straight, with not a single person walking through your frame. Hold the phone level, and good luck.
card.good_to_know: The Town Hall was built in stages between 1869 and 1889 in the Second Empire style, which gives it its pavilions and clock tower. It's heritage-listed and sits with the Queen Victoria Building and St Andrew's Cathedral. It also stands on the site of Sydney's first permanent cemetery, used from 1792 to 1820.

card.hook: Picture two stone towers standing flat-topped for decades, like a pair of unfinished sandcastles. They only got their spires in 2000, so St Mary's finally looks as grand as it always meant to.
card.stand_here: Head to Hyde Park, on the east side across College Street from the cathedral, and find the long reflecting pool. Check its exact spot on the map, then stand low and centred beside it, facing east toward the cathedral's western front.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if you're close to the pool and want both towers and the reflection in one shot. Use 1x from further back for a cleaner, less stretched look, and 2x to 5x for the spires and details, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the central tower on the middle line, then crouch and hold your phone low by the water so the reflection fills the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning is your friend, when the water is calmest and the light is soft. If the cathedral is lit up for Vivid Sydney, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the College Street forecourt near the main entrance stairs, facing Hyde Park, so the cathedral is right behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the low, centred end of the long pool, so the whole cathedral fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos outside are fine and no permit is needed for non-commercial shots. Keep it discreet, never photograph during services, and skip the flash around worshippers. Rules inside can vary, so check signs or the official site.
card.challenge: Catch the towers and their reflection so perfectly matched that your friends have to ask which way up the photo is.
card.good_to_know: St Mary's is Sydney's Catholic cathedral, designed by William Wardell, and building ran from 1866 to 1928. The twin spires on the front towers were only added in 2000. Before Hyde Park was parkland, the site was a barren patch where bricks were made for Governor Macquarie's buildings.

card.hook: Most people snap the MCA from the quayside and end up with a crowd of heads in the foreground. Climb up to Cahill Walk instead and the whole harbour-side scene opens up below you: pale stone, ferry wharves and water.
card.stand_here: Stand on Cahill Walk, the raised walkway above Circular Quay Station, and look down toward the MCA and West Circular Quay. The museum is to the north, so face north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the museum, the wharves and the water all in one frame. Then try 2x to pick out the clock tower and the stonework. Use 0.5x only if you want more of the walkway and quay, and keep straight lines away from the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the water's edge with a horizontal line so the building doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday light looking north can be harsh.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so more of the scene fits in. Turn so the museum is over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep a steady grip on your phone near railings, and don't stop where people need to walk past. Cahill Walk is a free public walkway, but access can change on special days like New Year's Eve, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Catch a ferry gliding through the bottom of your frame while the museum sits in the upper middle. Try a Live Photo, then pick your best frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The MCA fills a former Maritime Services Board building: six storeys of light orange-brown stone with a clock tower in the middle. A newer wing in black, white and brown stone was added when the museum reopened in 2012, so you see old and new side by side. The museum dates from 1991 and grew out of a bequest in the 1943 will of the artist JW Power. Some exhibitions may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Cahill Walk, the raised walkway above Circular Quay Station, and look down toward the MCA and West Circular Quay. The museum is to the north, so face north.

card.hook: Most people puff up Observatory Hill chasing the Harbour Bridge and stroll right past a sandstone building with its own time-ball tower. Give it a minute, because the park around it is the real photo prize.
card.stand_here: Stand in Observatory Park by the rotunda on the western side of the park, and turn back toward the observatory and the Harbour Bridge. Let the rotunda's columns or the old fig tree frame the view, with the Lower Fort Street terrace houses down in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the observatory. Go to zoom 0.5x for the bridge shot, so the terrace houses, the bridge and the sky all fit. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the building or the bridge on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the observatory on one of the lines, then tap the building or the bridge and nudge it darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, around 4-6pm. The western side of the park gets warm light on the bridge and The Rocks.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawns of Observatory Hill Park, on the grass beside the sandstone Observatory building. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, try 0.5x, and tilt so the building sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is open public space, but the observatory building may not be open at all times, so check the official site first if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Get the observatory and the fig tree's branches in one shot, with the branches along the edge like a picture frame.
card.good_to_know: The hilltop has been a windmill site, a fort and a signal station. The building you see now was designed by William Weaver and put up between 1857 and 1859. The time ball still drops every day at 1pm, and inside is a 29-centimetre refractor from 1874, the oldest telescope in regular use in Australia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Observatory Park by the rotunda on the western side of the park, and turn back toward the observatory and the Harbour Bridge. Let the rotunda's columns or the old fig tree frame the view, with the Lower Fort Street terrace houses down in front.

card.hook: Picture a tunnel of fig trees with a fountain at the start and a cathedral waiting at the far end. Hyde Park does that for you, and all you have to do is hold up your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Archibald Fountain at the north end of the park, where the two main walkways cross. Face south down the central avenue, so you get the fountain, St Mary's Cathedral behind it and the fig-lined path leading away.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain with the cathedral and avenue behind it. Try 0.5x to squeeze in the full canopy of fig trees, or 2x to pull the cathedral closer and tighten the avenue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the path along the centre line so the fig trees frame both sides, and keep the fountain in the lower third of the frame.
card.best_time: Sunset is described as especially lovely here. Early morning or late afternoon gives soft light, and arriving early helps with crowds.
card.selfie_here: Do it at the Archibald Fountain, which reviewers call a frequent selfie spot, with the cathedral spires making a strong backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the fountain and cathedral over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: A permit may be needed for some organised photography in City of Sydney parks, so check the official City of Sydney site if you're planning more than holiday snaps. Inside the Anzac Memorial building, keep it handheld and skip the flash.
card.challenge: Wait for a walker to stroll down the avenue, then catch them between the fig trees with the cathedral at the end.
card.good_to_know: Governor Macquarie set Hyde Park aside as open space in 1810, and it's the oldest public parkland in Australia. He named it after the Hyde Park in London. It covers about 16 hectares and has roughly 580 trees.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Archibald Fountain at the north end of the park, where the two main walkways cross. Face south down the central avenue, so you get the fountain, St Mary's Cathedral behind it and the fig-lined path leading away.

card.hook: Picture a tiny sandstone fortress parked in the middle of Sydney Harbour, like the world's grandest sandcastle. Better still, you can fit it, the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge into one shot.
card.stand_here: Head to Mrs Macquarie's Chair, the carved bench on the north-east edge of the point in the Royal Botanic Garden. Face north-east across the water, and Fort Denison will be right there in the middle of the harbour.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the fort, the Opera House and the Bridge all in one frame. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the tower. Use 0.5x only if you want the bench in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fort, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the sky and water keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or around sunset, when the light is warm on the Opera House and the harbour is usually calm.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x to squeeze in more background, and turn so a landmark sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face and take a few, because the fort is only a small shape on the water.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the chair on Mrs Macquarie's Point and shoot north-east, while you stand in front of them with the harbour view beyond you.
card.rules_and_safety: Fort Denison is closed to visitors for conservation works, so you'll be shooting it from the shore. Check current closures before you plan your day around it.
card.challenge: Put the fort on a lower gridline intersection, with the Opera House and Bridge on the other side of the frame, then see if you can keep all three perfectly lined up.
card.good_to_know: The island was once a rocky islet called Pinchgut, used to punish convicts, and its stone was later quarried for Circular Quay. The fort was finished in 1857 and named after Sir William Denison, then Governor of New South Wales. Its Martello tower is the only one ever built in Australia and the last built anywhere in the British Empire, and damage from the 1942 midget-submarine attack is still visible.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Mrs Macquarie's Chair, the carved bench on the north-east edge of the point in the Royal Botanic Garden. Face north-east across the water, and Fort Denison will be right there in the middle of the harbour.

card.hook: Apollo is up top, horses are spilling water below him, and even the tortoises are shooting jets like they've got a bus to catch. It's a lot of fun to photograph, and there's plenty of open space around it.
card.stand_here: Head for the north end of Hyde Park, on the path near the Archibald Fountain. From the park the fountain is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. For the St Mary's spires behind it, walk round to the far (west) side of the fountain and face east, then shuffle a few steps until the spires sit neatly behind the sculpture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big view of the fountain with the cathedral spires behind it. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the bronze figures and water jets. Use zoom 0.5x only when you're close and want the whole fountain in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sculpture or water, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the spray doesn't wash out to white.
card.best_time: Go just before sunset, when the light sparkles on the water spray. After dark the fountain is floodlit, so switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the paved area at the front of the fountain, around Birubi Circle in Hyde Park North, with the fountain behind you (check that name on the map). Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit above eye level so the bronze figures sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your photographer to stand about 10 to 15 metres back so the whole fountain fits, while you stand near the fountain. For the cathedral backdrop, they can turn so the St Mary's spires fill the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Water cascades around the Apollo figure and can soak anyone standing close, so step back if you're getting wet. The water may be switched off during conservation works, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, one shot down the tree-lined path with the fountain at the end, then one close-up of a tortoise or dolphin mid-spray. Can you catch the jet in action?
card.good_to_know: J. F. Archibald, owner and editor of The Bulletin magazine, left money in his will for the fountain and asked for a French artist. Sculptor François-Léon Sicard finished it in Paris in 1926, and it was unveiled in Sydney on 14 March 1932. Around the big basin you'll spot Artemis, Pan and Theseus, plus six tortoises and several dolphins.
